6
A surveyor’s device emits a pulse of light. The light is reflected from a wall 150 m away.
What is the total time taken for the pulse to travel from the device to the wall and then back to the
device?
A
0.05 ns
B
0.10 ns
C
0.50 s
D
1.0 s

hints: Notice the pulse must go to the wall 150 $\text{m}$ away and then return, so the total distance is $2 \times 150 \text{ m} = 300 \text{ m}$.
Connect this distance to the speed of light in air, $c \approx 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, using $t = s / v$.
Calculate $300 / (3.0 \times 10^8)$ in $\text{s}$, then convert to $\mu\text{s}$ and check why $\text{ns}$ options are far too small.
walkthrough: Identify the journey: device to wall is 150 $\text{m}$, wall back to device is another 150 $\text{m}$, so total distance $s = 300 \text{ m}$.
State the governing rule: light travels at $c \approx 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, and for uniform speed $t = s / v$.
Set up the calculation: $t = 300 \text{ m} / (3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1})$.
Check units and prefix: $10^{-6} \text{ s} = 1.0 \mu\text{s}$, whereas $1 \text{ ns} = 10^{-9} \text{ s}$, so the nanosecond options are 10000 times too small.
Note that $0.50 \mu\text{s}$ would be the time for 150 $\text{ m}$ only, without the return trip. This is option D.

A.explanation: Too small by a factor of about 20000. It confuses $\text{ns}$ with $\mu\text{s}$ and misses the factor of 2 for the return journey.

B.explanation: Too small by a factor of about 10000. It uses a nanosecond scale instead of a microsecond scale for 300 $\text{m}$ travel at the speed of light.

C.explanation: This is the one-way time for 150 $\text{m}$. It omits doubling the distance for travel to the wall and back to the device.

D.explanation: The round-trip distance $300 \text{ m}$ divided by $3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ gives $1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s} = 1.0 \mu\text{s}$.
